author: charlesrt
text:
What
GOV.UK needs a Dark Mode theme.
Why
I have written about why Dark Mode should be an inclusive design consideration.
2018: The Dark (Mode) Web Rises
2017: Apple Need a Dark Mode
2016: Molly Watt
Anything else
Some of the suggestions I've poked at in the past have always come with added complications. For example, how do we include an accessibility toolbar in a way that benefits the users who need it without getting in the way of those who don't.
The preference has always been to allow users to change website themes based on their own preferences using third-party and browser tools. This has always left a gap on mobile devices and often requires extra digital skill.
Safari Technology Preview has recently added a CSS media query prefers-color-scheme which can detect the system-level preference in MacOS Mojave of a light or dark theme. You can now easily write CSS custom to both and the user only has to declare a preference once to affect all websites (providing them adopt it).
Adoption and sharing of this by big websites (GOV.UK) will help spread awareness and prompt other platforms to add their own system-level preferences.
Check out a prototype: https://govuk-dark-mode.herokuapp.com. You'll need Safari Technology Preview and MacOS Mojave at time of raising this issue.

author: NickColley
text:
Thanks for putting this together it's pretty exciting to see the progress 👍
We currently have the following documented for what we do to try and help users who need to change their colours:

We aim to support users who adjust or override the colours of websites they visit. We test this by changing colours in Firefox, by enabling 'High Contrast' mode in Windows and by using the High Contrast plugin for Chrome.

We have also blogged about this here:
https://accessibility.blog.gov.uk/2018/08/01/supporting-users-who-change-colours-on-gov-uk/
It'd be also worth considering the dark mode for Windows which my assumption is has a much higher use than this, at the same time. There's a related bug for that here: alphagov/govuk-frontend#937
The biggest risk I see from Apple's approach is that if we implement this feature it'll be inconsistently applied across GOV.UK (as most of GOV.UK will not have an up-to-date version of the GOV.UK Design System). Since other dark modes force interfaces to be dark, even if the website has not 'opted-in'
We need to decide if having Apple's dark mode work inconsistently, out weighs that con.

author: charlesrt
text:
Thanks, Nick. The work done to make GOV.UK accessible to users who change their colours, contrast, etc is great 👍
I’m excited about ‘prefers-color-scheme’ as it lets us control the way this affects the content on GOV.UK, and because the changes would be made through CSS there shouldn’t be any issues like when colours are overridden by plugins, etc (to be clear: I don’t intend that we stop work to make it work for users who override in this way at that might always be a thing).
It’s worth saying that this isn’t an Apple dark mode thing. At the moment this only works in Safari Tech Preview if you are running MacOS Mojave but it’s part of a suite of ‘prefers-‘ media queries that we should expect to come to all browsers soon. I assume that once implemented in a browser available on Windows it will automatically honour a system-level Dark Mode preference set on Windows.
It’s my assumption that this be a wildly implemented on all major platforms and we can be dark-mode-ready, if you like.
I reckon this is an interesting piece of work because we’re talking about setting a preference for an appearance theme rather than overridden and declare precise colours. It’ll involve collaborative work in the community to create a Dark theme and decide what should and shouldn’t change along with adjustments to our colour palette and perhaps even typography as reading experience on dark backgrounds is slightly different.
All of GOV.UK not running the latest version of the Design System is a problem (some satire: a few years ago we spent a lot of effort to replace hundreds of different government websites with one, (feels) more like maintaining hundreds of different government websites on one domain that all look the same but under the hood are individual).
Embedding this as part of the Design System as a considered theme is definitely a must. For older parts of the website they may need manual adjustment. It only took me an hour to hack the prototype kit style sheet to achieve an indicative appearance. It shouldn’t take more than that for a team to do the same for their service. Getting them to do so and release it however may be a policatal challenge.
Lots to think about 🤔

The twitter thread commented above shows a screenshot where the Chrome app UI is still Light (presumably as it hasn’t been updated with the functionality) and that this could be confusing.
There is also the suggestion that people might want a Dark UI but Light content. It’s hard to know for sure what people say vs what they’d do. Presently, this isn’t even an option as the preference is declared singularly at system-level. Maybe Apple (and others) will include this sort of choice in the future and ‘prefers-color-scheme’ will take its value from the preference set for content. We need to focus on what’s within our gift.
When considering the implementation of this, we should prioritise the preference set by a user who needs to view content in Dark vs aesthetic preference.

author: Nooshu
text:
Auto Dark Mode (Chrome)
The Google Chrome team are currently working on a new browser feature in Desktop and Android Chrome called "Auto Dark Mode".
Links

Chrome Platform Status ticket
Specification
Small User Research Poll
Chrome blog post

Context
It is currently only being rolled out as an origin trial, meaning it will only be available on websites who have opted in to test the feature.
Issue
On Wednesday 26th Jan 2022 the GOV.UK team received a report that GOV.UK looked "broken" when this feature was enabled and a discussion was had in the day's Frontend Community meeting. The user must have 'forced' Chrome into this mode using the chrome://flags settings and searching for "darken websites", so it is currently highly unlikely that any user will run into these issues.
But it does raise a number of questions:

Whose job is it to "fix" these issues?

Is this lead by the GOV.UK team or the Design System team?


Should we even need (or try) to fix these issues, or should it be left up to the Chrome team and specification body to resolve?
What accessibility issues will be raised if the colours are changed?

How are these going to be "fixed" and then tested?



It also raises usability issues that are almost impossible to fix when a user moves across services. For example, if a user has "Dark Mode" auto enabled for "www.gov.uk" this setting won't be persistent across services (since cookies can't be shared between www.gov.uk and *.service.gov.uk). This also brings up the issue that since its application is algorithmic and decided via the browser, what happens if different services use different versions of GOV.UK Frontend (or even not use it at all)? It could be that the browser chooses different colours per service.
It's also worth mentioning that the feature comes with lots of options (see screenshot below). It is still unclear as to how (or if) this will be presented to a user, and will they be able to choose each of these options individually.

Options
Options we have at the moment:
Do nothing
Here we don't change anything for the moment and wait to see the results from the Origin trial. It could be that it simply isn't a feature that users want or need, and Chrome pulls the plug on the feature all together.  So any work will be wasted time and effort.
Opt-out of Auto Dark Theme using a meta tag, CSS or per-element CSS
The Chrome team allows developers to opt out of the application of the Auto Dark Theme using the following meta tag added to a page <head>:
<meta name="color-scheme" content="only light">
It is also possible to do this via CSS, for everything, or per-element:
:root {
  color-scheme: only light;
}

#my-element {
  color-scheme: only light;
}
This gives a team the time to decide on the best option to select, and maybe even time to develop our own dark theme (which will override this feature entirely).
The blog post even recommends writing your own dark theme:

We strongly recommend implementing your own curated dark theme instead, in order to respect the user's preference and keep those benefits

Recommendation
At the moment, I feel we should do nothing with "Auto Dark Mode" and wait to see if it is accepted by users. This is backed up by the fact that a small Twitter poll I ran show users don't even know it exists at the moment.
If it is that we start getting more reports of pages looking "broken" I'd recommend we consider using the meta tag or CSS to temporarily disable the browser algorithm and then get involved in providing this user feedback to the Google Chrome team via the link they have provided.
Ultimately, I think time would be better spent on developing our own "dark theme" than chasing bugs in a single browser's "auto implementation".

author: IeuanParkerDBT
text: Hi @joelanman here's a gif of what the prototype does. Very simple, but what this does is change the website theme based on the theme set on your OS. So, for instance if a user had their OS theme in Dark, the gov website would change based on the preference set. One of the reasons we thought about doing it this way was the ease of implementing. Because we want this to span all gov services, we thought instead of having toggles or buttons displayed, and us needing to put those buttons in, we would allow the operating system to set the theme. This helps the user as well in the sense that they know where to go to change the theme if needed, as different services would have different button location for the toggle/button. Forgot to mention also, this is a simple CSS change using the @media css rule, with no javascript involved.

author: RobinKnipe

In a lot of implementations of a govuk dark mode (and light mode), I see colours being explicitly set for various elements and classes; would it not be better to just set the default color and background-color on the body (with the prefers media query), then focus on the rarer cases of coloured elements and text (panels, links, buttons, etc.)?
I guess I'm asking specifically in the context of trying to honour the user's OS suggested theme - and not for the cases where a proper govuk theme is being created (e.g. offered as a choice as part of a site-specific a11y feature).
I ask because I'm likely going to have to hack this together myself (for UKRI), so I share the sentiment that I'd rather be using something more authoritative from GDS or the Design System!

author: stevenjmesser
text:
Hypothesis: rolling out dark mode across the GOV.‌UK ecosystem could be harder than rolling out the crown.
There’s a higher degree of visual change, which makes inconsistencies more jarring. For example, if you move between GOV.‌UK guidance in dark mode, a service in light mode, then jump to an account in dark mode, you’re really going to notice the difference. GOV.‌UK is supposed to feel like one thing, but this will certainly break that. (The crown is comparatively small and easier to miss.)
It could be harder to create consistency across the ecosystem for dark mode, which requires good comms and services to act on that comms. Alternatively there would need to be a central directive in order to ensure the journeys which most commonly traverse departmental boundaries are consistent.
We possibly won’t be able to tackle this in a user-friendly way until we have cross-government data from the Single Data Environment. However, it may be possible for small, closed-boundary services (like internal services, case management systems, intranets, etc.) to make advances.

author: Gramatter-DIT
text:
Hi @stevenjmesser the solution we proposed within the Firebreak project negates this. The beauty of the way in which we've approached this is that the user will have defined the setting within their operating system so the default state for each GOV.UK website would be already chosen by the user, whether it be dark or light. Thus, they'd be accustomed to this environment.
There are no interactions made by button toggling which would potentially cause jarring visual inconsistencies.
All that's needed is a simple line of code added to the CSS of each GOV.UK site to accept this user choice. I realise logistically it may be some work to do this to each and every site, but in this instance, the positives outweigh the negatives, making for a more user-inclusive experience.

author: stevenjmesser
text:
Thanks for the reply, @Gramatter-DIT, but I don't think that would work.
Imagine the following scenario:

www.gov.uk adopts a future release of GOV.UK Frontend with support for dark mode.
Service 1 uses GOV.UK Frontend v3.12, which does not support dark mode.
Service 2 adopts a future release of GOV.UK Frontend with support for dark mode.
A user navigates from content on www.gov.uk to Service 1. After using Service 1, the user navigates to Service 2.

Despite the user's browser settings asking for dark mode styling from all 3 websites, only www.gov.uk and Service 2 support dark mode, meaning that Service 1 appears in light mode. This presents a broken, inconsistent experience for the user.
What do you think? Have I missed something?

author: RobinKnipe
text:
'@stevenjmesser the behaviour you've described is basically that of the entire internet right now, because many sites have made the effort to honour dark-mode preferences while others have not. Until the whole of the internet catches up with the vanguard there will be an uncomfortable mix, but that's not a reason to abandon the pursuit of a much requested feature with many benefits.
The approach described by @Gramatter-DIT (which I assume uses the prefers-color-scheme CSS media feature) should be the goal here, as this will empower the user to make the choice of styling. It would also support themes that follow light conditions and transition between light and dark mode states to better complement the user's environment.
I appreciate the desire to maintain the consistent look and feel of the gov pages, but the focus of this effort should be on other colours and branding that can be consistent between the styles. The current simplicity and reduced colour palette of the gov styling already lends itself to supporting both modes.

author: stevenjmesser
text:
'@RobinKnipe Thanks for the reply!

the behaviour you've described is basically that of the entire internet right now, because many sites have made the effort to honour dark-mode preferences while others have not.

I see what you're saying but I don't think we should compare the GOV.‌UK ecosystem of services to the entire web. They're not comparable domains. The goal of GOV.‌UK is that it feels like 'one thing' to a user, whereas that is not the goal of the entire web.
What we're not saying is that we won't look at making dark mode available, but we do need to think through a release strategy that ensures consistency for users traversing multiple services in one journey.

I suppose there's a question as to when problems like that become ours to solve.
There are users who, conversely, find plain black on plain white to be easier to read than more muted colours or inverse/dark modes. While I do understand that “Gov.uk should be visually consistent” aspect mentioned by @stevenjmesser above, we wouldn’t take an approach of “we won’t implement it anywhere until we can implement it everywhere” with some less visually-apparent aspect of accessibility — and we users who have an OS-preference set to prefers-color-scheme: dark are very accustomed to experiences flitting between the 2.

author: querkmachine
text:
'@solidgoldpig The mention of being able to change colours in the accessibility statement is in reference to the user being able to do that using their browser or device settings without the GOV.UK website preventing it.
It's not a claim that the website provides that functionality; just as it doesn't provide the functionality to zoom or read things aloud. These functions are better provided by the user's device than anything we could do within the confines of a webpage.

author: stuarttaylor-sys
text:
Can we just take a moment to appreciate that this issue was opened on Dec 3, 2018
Dec 2018: Microsoft announces Edge will switch to the Chromium engine.
Jan 2021: The aspect-ratio CSS property, replacing old padding hacks.
Mar 2021: The Interop Project launches. Major browsers commit to fixing web standard compatibility issues.
Feb 2022: Cascade Layers (@layer) in all major browsers to fix CSS wars.
Aug 2022: Chrome 105 introduces Container Queries and the :has() parent selector.
Dec 2023: Firefox completes cross-browser support for :has(), making it fully production-ready.
Apr 2023: Chrome ships native CSS Nesting.
May 2023: The native HTML popover attribute rolls out in Chrome
Sep 2023: Safari 17 adds support for subgrid
Jul 2024: Chrome ships field-sizing: content, enabling auto-expanding textareas without JavaScript.
Mid 2025: Scroll-Driven Animations achieve cross-browser stability.
2026: Advanced programmatic CSS functions (like inline if() conditionals) enter the chat.
This got kicked so hard into the long grass, the whole web has changed since.

author: querkmachine
text:
'@stuarttaylor-sys And govuk-frontend still supports pre-Chromium Edge, because government services need to serve as many users as possible, including those living on the long tail of older and less capable hardware and software.
The lack of a dark mode landing in Frontend isn't because of a lack of motivation, but because it's difficult to do without creating a degraded experience for real (often vulnerable) people.

author: stuarttaylor-sys
text:
I fully appreciate the commitment to accessibility, and protecting the long tail of users on legacy hardware or frozen mobile webviews (like pre-Chromium Edge and older Android devices). Serving vulnerable citizens must always take priority over visual trends. 100%
However... When a design system tries to force a single codebase to serve a modern smartphone and a 12-year-old library computer simultaneously, it creates a web of "lowest common denominator".
Given the massive shifts in CSS capabilities and browser rendering engines since this issue was opened in December 2018, we could now separate how the design system code is written from how individual service teams choose to deploy it. So  instead of introducing a breaking change or forcing heavy polyfills onto low-end devices, the govuk-frontend could unblock dark mode (and other modern CSS features) by moving to a multi-file asset distribution model. One size does not fit anyone particularly well after all.
A style-sheet for the legacy and an opt-in stylesheet that each service could adopt based on their userbase.

author: joelanman
text:
I think it would be useful to the discussion to understand more about the risks of implementing dark mode. If we restrict it to just supporting the system setting, what would be bad outcomes? I can think of a couple:

Users on unsupported browsers wouldn't get dark mode
As users move between gov.uk sites, some would support dark mode and some wouldn't

I'm not sure 1 is a risk - thats just the situation they have now. 2 is unfortunate but it's an inevitable outcome of our distributed approach - we see similar issues in take up of the new brand. I would argue the value people would get from many sites (hopefully including the main publishing platform) supporting it would outweigh the downside of the inconsistency between sites.

author: NickColley
text:
As users move between gov.uk sites, some would support dark mode and some wouldn't

This is a big one, since moving between dark mode and white mode could be confusing or even visually stressful.
It is a similar issue to the new brand but in my opinion it's much more jarring to go from dark to white vs a slightly different brand.
I have considered perhaps you could introduce a dark mode that's ready to go, then at a later date actually turn it on.
For example, in version 10.0.0 dark mode is 'ready' but only when the most popular projects are on 10.0.0 is there a release to actually enable dark mode e.g. 10.1.0. Then the 'roll out' would be to just redeploy applications.
In terms of other hard problems to solve, consider that it is likely that we'd want to allow users to configure if the dark mode is enabled based on the operating system, or forced to dark or light. Also I think it might be appropriate to allow users to specify the amount of contrast e.g. a 'subtle dark mode' and a 'high contrast mode'.
How do we keep those settings consistent across GOV.UK websites? Where does the user actually configure that?
One other one is the GOV.UK Design System could be dark mode ready but tons of valid custom code exists that users have made to compliment the Design System exists, so we'd need to advocate and make it easy for people to make their custom code work in dark mode. Probably another good reason to have dark mode exist before actually 'turning it on'.

author: kubabartwicki
text:
Hello
We are starting a discussion about emerging design patterns for utilising AI in public services. This probably mostly covers generative AI, but other design patterns for making use of machine learning, data science, and similar technologies are also useful.
We’re doing this because there is a lot here! Many teams across government are experimenting with AI, and we are working out how to design for this. We need to work out how to surface AI-generated content to users, how to talk to them about accuracy, and how to design more dynamic interactions. A space to share learnings in the open seems like a good place to start 🥁
I work on the GOV.UK AI team, where we are experimenting how AI can help people navigate the complexity of government services and information. We have a ton of insights from testing so far, and we know that other teams do too. Most of our learnings come from experimenting with GOV.UK Chat. You can learn more about that in this blog post, or drop us a message if you want to chat more about it.
We’ll start by sharing some of our insights, but please join the discussion if you work in government and have things to share. Keep in mind that it’s all work in progress, and evolving fast!

threadTitle: AI — we want your input (emerging patterns, use cases, research findings)
author: LucyMcArthur-GDS
text:
Describing accuracy limitations in an AI chat
Generative AI can sometimes show inaccurate information with a high degree of authority. We’ve been learning lots about how to communicate this and make sure users don’t follow inaccurate advice.
In the GOV.UK Chat experiment, we’ve had some success explaining accuracy limitations in a chat conversation, as part of the onboarding. Showing onboarding as messages received from the chat was a lot more effective than displaying the content on a static page. It also allows us to break the information down into shorter messages without overwhelming users.
We are also experimenting with integrating actions into the chat interface. During the onboarding, the bottom area of the chat shows two buttons. Once you’ve onboarded, this changes to include a text input field. Users responded really well to having rich UI elements in the chat, and it’s a pattern we want to build on. We have some really interesting content insights on this which we’ll share soon too.

threadTitle: AI — we want your input (emerging patterns, use cases, research findings)
author: LucyMcArthur-GDS
text:
Checking answers
We also need to give users a really clear next step to do what they’re trying to do, and to make it easy for them to verify information generated by AI.
In our chat experiments, we are integrating a “check this answer” step in the user journey. This includes links to relevant GOV.UK guidance pages directly after chat’s responses. In research, we found that links were viewed as a way to find further information, but not always as a checking step, so we made this more prominent. Checking content isn’t a typical user behaviour within digital tools, but using a prominent “check this answer” component with a warning icon helped encourage it.
To make this more intuitive, we are also exploring things like linking people to specific parts of pages, or highlighting relevant content snippets.

threadTitle: AI — we want your input (emerging patterns, use cases, research findings)
author: romanidavies
text:
We have been working on a white label version of the AI assistant created for caseworker guidance.
We have replaced the content of our designs with a general subject matter. This subject matter is 'Superhero applications', however we hope this will still illustrate the design decisions made.
It can be found here: https://github.com/LandRegistry/ai-assistant-whitelabel
For context:
Within HMLR, Andy Porter, Kit Harding and I have been developing a ‘design language’ for AI UI.
There has been very little validation or usability testing or feedback from users at this time. We appreciate this is a completely new paradigm, and we don’t have gov patterns yet so wanted to share our progress.
We’ve been working on:

General look and feel like layout, colours
What language to use- what to name things, how to describe things- including a how to ask/ use AI
New components/patterns

Within these files we have included some insight into the decisions made. They are duplicated here:
Guidance homepage:
We needed to consider how the assistant could be integrated with the existing caseworker guidance system.

Within the scope of this project, we had limited capacities to amend the existing guidance interface, therefore we had to take this into consideration of our own designs. The keyword search was already present.
We added a new lead paragraph to the page, to inform users they could search by two ways and ensured both search methods had equal weighting. It was important to present the methods equally but also try to encourage users to use the assistant.
We came up with a 'widget-like' component to represent the assistant, which could be minimised for other pages in the guidance. However, on the homepage the widget is fully expanded for maximum engagement. This widget has the same visual language as the assistant. We have included a realistic, common example question, to help users understand how to use the tool and consider how it could help their work. It was important that this example used natural language to demonstrate this benefit of interacting with the assistant.
As we are encouraging users to check the responses using the existing keyword search, the assistant opens in a new tab.
Caseworker guidance article page
Following a keyword search on the homepage, users are taken to a search results page where they can then select the appropriate article from the shortlisted view.

We believe that if users are unable to easily find the information using the traditional, keyword search, they may consider utilising the tool. Therefore, users can launch the assistant from this article page.
On this page, we have added the minimised widget to this page. The widget has been minimised by removing the example text. The visual language and proactive, encouraging tone remains.
A future consideration could be that if the assistant is launched from this page, the context of the article could be passed to the model, initiating the search.
Casework guidance AI assistant- homepage
The homepage of the assistant is minimal. We have tried to focus the user on a simple interaction- asking a question.

We have told users the assistant uses AI, which is important from an ethical perspective. This clause involved a lot of wider conversations, to balance the ethical responsibility of informing users of the AI usage but also that the information supplied should be checked.
To label the button we considered alternatives such as 'Ask', 'Search' and 'Ask a question'. As a conversational interface we were unsure of the language that is best suited for this component. For the first iteration, we have used 'Go'.
The LLM has been designed to allow users to have 4 question 'conversations'. This means the LLM will consider the context of up to 4 previous questions to inform the following response. Up to 4 questions was considered the optimal number of questions, that best informed the LLM without degrading the quality of responses.
The secondary link, 'Assist with another query', starts a new 'conversation' removing all previous context.
Normally, we wouldn't explain how to use a tool. However, considering this new paradigm of design, underpinned by our user research we felt there was a user need to provide guidance. Our user research found that our users didn't know how to interact with the assistant and as a result, the quality of responses were poor.
Therefore, we have included links to the purpose built guidance and demonstrations to help our users understand how to best ask questions. These materials have been tested and iterated following exposure to users.
Casework guidance AI assistant- query
Upon entering a query into the assistant, the assistant generates a response using source information from the articles in the existing caseworker guidance system. It then considers the information found and generates a response, with the source information extracted from the articles available for users to check the AI generated response.

The conversation is left aligned, as the assistant will only be used on desktop. This also felt more appropriate to follow the users likely reading habits on desktop (from top to bottom). We made the assumption that as the responses are likely to be large blocks of text, they would be easier to read.
Also, we have chosen to not name the questions and responses (indicating 'who was speaking') as it felt that this added an informality to the conversation, which contradicts the subject matter and use cases.
The content on the right hand panel remains consistent.
Casework guidance AI assistant- additional queries
Our system is able to take context from up to 4 queries when generating responses. Therefore, we had to consider how multiple related queries and responses could be displayed.

One way we distinguish between the question and response is the text widths. The users question is displayed at 1/3 width, as it is likely the response will be much longer. In addition to this, the question is on #D2E2F1, whilst the response is on govuk-colour("light-grey") #f3f2f1- these colours have been used on the GOV.UK Chat (experimental). There is a small gap between the boxes to create another visual difference between the question and response.
Casework guidance AI assistant- inline feedback
Following the response, we have introduced inline feedback to allow the user to feed back on the helpfulness of the response.

Initially, the team were keen to introduce a 'thumbs up'/'thumbs down' mechanism to gain feedback on the response. We were aware of the accessibility limitations that this would introduce and therefore considered current feedback approaches, specifically on the GOV.UK chat. Following this, we explored 'When you have finished, tell us if the answer was useful'. However, this approach did not allow feedback on a 'repsonse by response' basis, rather the conversation as a whole, which was too broad.
Further conversations confirmed the objective for the team was to recieve definitive feedback to the helpfulness of the response, which could then indicate further explorations into inaccurately generated responses. The 'yes'/'no' question allowed the team to be able to pinpoint inaccurate responses to improve the LLM.

We provided the team with visually hidden text for the 'yes'/'no' links to ensure they could be understood by assistive technology.


Upon selecting 'yes'/'no' the inline text changes to ask a follow up question asking if the user would like to expand on why the response was helpful/unhelpful.
We considered which pair of words would be appropriate for a positive/negative response. This included 'useful'/'not useful', 'correct'/'incorrect', 'helpful'/'unhelpful', 'accurate'/'inaccurate', 'like'/'dislike'. We don't know which word pair works best for users as we were unable to test these but we thought 'helpful'/'unhelpful' were best as it allows users to consider their own context whereas 'correct'/'incorrect' is too absolute. For example, a response could be factually correct but does not specifically answer the users response or vice versa.


By selecting the links following the repsonses, users are taken to one of these pages where they can provide details about why a response was helpful or unhelpful. This is optional, users do not need to add this additional detail for us to record the initial helpful/unhelpful response. The question is tailored depending on if a user answered 'yes' or 'no'.
Casework guidance AI assistant- general feedback
As with any new tool, we are keen to facilitate users submitting feedback. This feedback is also important to improve our LLM.

To make it easier for users to submit feedback, we provide users with a free text field, rather than asking specific questions.
This is accessible through the right hand panel on the assistant's interface. Users can access this at any point during their journey. This is important as some of our users may want to feedback at a more convenient time (rather than following specific responses). We have tailored this question to be more general, to allow users to reflect on their experience using the tool as a whole. We're following the principles of the 'Tell us how to improve this service' pattern.

threadTitle: AI — we want your input (emerging patterns, use cases, research findings)
author: andrewmclean-hmrc
text:
Hi, I'm wondering if the GOV.UK chat project has explored any established industry conversation design patterns. I'm chiefly thinking about Acknowledgement, Confirmation, Prompt that's the "mantra" pattern for Hans Van Dam at the Conversation Design Institute.
The pattern is designed to build trust and confidence in users by showing them that the AI has heard them, understood them and wants to be helpful (similar to an interaction with a live call agent).
An example might be:
User: I want to register for VAT
AI: Ok, here's how to register for VAT. Gives them answer. Is there anything else I can help with?
In this example:
Acknowledgement = Ok (user feels they've been heard)
Confirmation = here's how to register for VAT (this would be an implicit confirmation - AI has over 50% confidence in its understanding of the query. Explicit confirmation would try to get the user to confirm the ask if the AI was less confident)
Prompt = Is there anything else I can help with? (user's turn and also way to keep them on task)
This pattern's widely used by, among others:

Klarna
Bank of America
KLM
Sephora
Domino's

As I say, just looking to understand if this kind of pattern has been researched. I'm keen to look at it for Ask HMRC online as we move to a Contact Centre as a Service platform. So any insight you might have would be useful.
Cheers

author: dodi1978
text:
Hi all, I just came across this forum and wanted to jump in from a slightly different angle. I am not a designer by the way, but an academic whose research interfaces with conversation design. Here is my portfolio: https://portfoliodippold.netlify.app/
I've been researching how people experience AI chat in public services - specifically looking at rapport, i.e. that sense of warmth, trust and being understood (or not) when you're talking to a chatbot. My fieldwork has been on an NHS AI chat system used for cervical screening booking, but my findings are relevant to the kinds of questions you're raising here.
My main point perhaps: language matters! Just a few highlights:

Choice-oriented language landed really well. Repetitive, inflexible or imperative messaging (even when well-intentioned, e.g. nudging someone to complete a step) came across as pushy and actually put people off engaging further.
This mattered a lot more for users with prior trauma, anxiety, or who were otherwise more vulnerable - which feels relevant given how much of gov AI chat touches sensitive, high-stakes stuff (health, benefits, legal status...).
I pulled this together into a taxonomy of six "rapport dimensions" (goals, autonomy, attention, face, fairness, ethicality) that might work as a lightweight heuristic alongside other content design principles you are using.  whatever accuracy/content design principles you're developing.
I have attached a policy brief I have recently put together based on my work, which also features the rapport taxonomy. Happy to talk you though it if anyone is interested!

threadTitle: Observed issues under Safari's Adaptive Dark Mode
author: querkmachine
text: The Safari 27.3 beta (on iOS and iPadOS) has introduced a feature called [‘Adaptive Dark Mode’](https://webkit.org/blog/18541/introducing-adaptive-dark-mode/) (henceforth, ADM) that coerces pages without dark modes into the dark side. It does this by detecting whether a page has been given a dark mode by the author by checking for the presence of the `color-scheme` meta tag and CSS property. When the user’s device is using the dark system theme, and they visit a website without a dark mode for the first time, they are prompted whether they want to turn on Adaptive Dark Mode. If they choose to do so it’s turned on for all websites, not just the website the user enabled it on, and remains active so long as the they’re using the dark system theme. In flicking through GOV.UK and the Design System with it turned on, I’ve not noticed many issues (unlike [Chrome’s equivalent feature](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/2582)), but for reference sake, I'm writing them down anyway. Like Chrome's Auto Dark Mode, this is technically still in a pre-release state, so things might change prior to release. ## Issues what I found ### Focus styles Focus styles are somewhat inconsistent. It seems like ADM maintains the background and box-shadow colour of focus styles, but will change the text colour. What colour it actually uses was a little inconsistent, I noticed it using both white and grey. ### Buttons Secondary buttons have had both the background and box-shadow colours inverted, making them look a bit unusual. More like text with an underline than a button. I'm not confident that the colour combination it comes up with for warning buttons is ideal. Whilst just about meeting WCAG minimum contrast (it's basically dead on 4.5:1), perceptually it feels like white text would still provide better contrast in this context. ### Text input, Textarea Text inputs and textareas render with an inverted black background, however the border colour is not inverted, making empty inputs appear as ominous black voids. Prefixes and suffixes _do_ have their borders inverted, however. ## Notification banner The border colours of banners are modified to be lighter, but the normally colour matched heading backgrounds are not. ### Warning text The warning text 'icon' doesn't have its colour adapted, making it less visually prominent in ADM. ### File upload The native (non-enhanced) system file input has quite a dark button. ### Other noticings The heuristics around which pseudo-elements it converts is a bit off sometimes. For example, the pseudo-element that makes the GOV.UK mega menu and search appear full width doesn’t change colour.

threadTitle: Observed issues under Chrome's Auto Dark Mode
author: querkmachine
text:
Since Chrome version 78, Google has included an experimental feature in the browser, initially named "Forced Dark Mode" and, as of writing, named "Auto Dark Mode for Web Content". 

This feature automatically modifies the appearance of webpages in order to create a "dark mode" version. This is done even if the page already supplies a "dark mode" via the `prefers-color-scheme` CSS media query. It also appears to ignore the `color-scheme` property. 

The flag comes with several different "enabled" modes (as of Chrome 99), which modify how Chrome is internally applying changes. Each mode results in subtly (sometimes radically) different resulting colours.

1. Enabled
2. Enabled with simple HSL-based inversion
3. Enabled with simple CIELAB-based inversion
4. Enabled with simple RGB-based inversion
5. Enabled with selective image inversion
6. Enabled with selective inversion of non-image elements
7. Enabled with selective inversion of everything
8. Enabled with increased text contrast

Most of these modes appear to work by first overriding neutral light background colours (such as white and light greys), and modifying any copy that it detects as existing on a modified background colour to maintain suitable contrast. Most other colours appear to be left intact. This method of alteration means that colours are not all modified in the same way: `$govuk-brand-color` in mode 1, for example, is unmodified when used as a background or border colour (#1d70b8), but is changed when it is used as a text colour (#61a1ee).

Mode 4 appears to simply invert all colours on the page, regardless of usage. 

I'm not sure how mode 1 is different from the others. It may be that this is an "automatic" mode where Chrome tries to determine which of the other seven modes works best for the given page and uses that one.

We have received at least one bug report raised by a user who was using Chrome's Auto Dark Mode feature for accessibility reasons (to make content easier to read with cataracts).

> RE the dark mode, it is now a function in Google Chrome that you can activate and it will force a dark version if the website can accommodate it. Not everyone does, BBC News for example still comes through with a traditional black text on a white background – but it works for many.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
In Google Chrome, go to `chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark` (this should jump you straight to "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents") and enable the flag.

## Actual vs expected behaviour
Currently, a number of these modes produce colour combinations which fail the contrast requirements established in WCAG 2.1. 

Below is a non-exhaustive subset of issues currently identified in Auto Dark Mode.

### Text inputs and textareas
Text inputs are displayed with a grey background and black border in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8. This fails to meet the expected 1:3 contrast ratio for UI elements (at 1:1.68). 

![Screenshot of the design system input component, appearing grey on black.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644743-7632dc27-cc56-4558-bd40-8fee1109717c.png)

They are displayed with a light grey background and white border in modes 3 and 5, which easily meets contrast ratio expectations.

They are displayed with the default white background and black border in all other modes.

### Input prefixes and suffixes

These are difficult to read in modes 2 and 4, where they are black on a dark grey background (1:3.23).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example, where the text is black on dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160646813-ac2ad0a1-083d-4ca0-b571-b1ecacd450e4.png)

These are much more difficult to read in modes 3 and 5, which renders it as black on an even darker grey (1.22).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example. The text is visually imperceptible from the background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650473-9c6f3529-5a06-4408-b20e-242b1c66a08e.png)

These are displayed with adequate contrast in other modes.

### Checkboxes and radio buttons
The border and selection states of checkboxes and radio buttons do not have sufficient contrast in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8 (at a pretty much imperceptible contrast ratio of 1:1.04)

![Screenshot of the design system checkbox component, illustrating insufficient contrast between the checkboxes and background, which are both dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644218-1fc50370-249e-4e47-b73a-eab9a8b8ea34.png)

They are displayed with white borders and selection states in all other modes.

### Select

In modes 1, 6, 7, and 8, select boxes are rendered with a dark grey background and dark grey border (1:1.04).

![Screenshot of the design system select component, which appears to just be white text with no border or icon.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160648934-5554f80a-1794-40e1-a9b7-a7c16df83d29.png)

They are rendered with a black background and white border in all other modes.

### Skiplinks

In modes 1, 2, 6, and 7, skiplinks are rendered as white on focus-colour yellow, which does not meet contrast requirements (1:1.34).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649767-19aecf58-2ea6-4517-9852-283a4c91f922.png)

In mode 4, it is white on light blue, which is also below expectations (1:3.24).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright blue background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649982-3f7999be-3540-40c5-8d00-7b9350407360.png)

In mode 8, it is white on focus-color yellow, but additionally has a black text shadow/stroke effect applied, which makes it difficult to read.

![Screenshot of a white link with a thin, pixellated black shadow surrounding it, on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650309-a61034bd-d400-4ca3-b312-db890c382f19.png)

This is displayed with adequate contrast (albeit, in white on brown) in all other modes.

### Iconography

Most iconography fails to meet contrast requirements in virtually all modes. This includes:
- the open and close arrows on the Accordion component.
- the arrow on the Back link component.
- the arrows on the Breadcrumbs component.
- the exclamation icon on the Warning text component.

### Other components
The good news is that, for the most part, the majority of other components we have in GOV.UK Frontend are not as badly affected as those above, with various components such as Inset text, Error summary, and Notification banner maintaining their necessary visual presence and suitable contrast even with modified colours. 

## Environment
The results specified here were taken in Chrome 99, running on macOS 15.3, whilst the operating system was set to light mode. 

Interestingly, Chrome DevTools does not give any indication that a change to the page's appearance has taken place. All HTML and CSS content, including the user agent stylesheet, computed styles, and those returned through JavaScript, appear unmodified and are not aligned with the page's actual appearance when Auto Dark Mode is enabled.

threadTitle: Observed issues under Chrome's Auto Dark Mode
author: querkmachine
text:
Chrome (as of writing, version 144) appears to have changed the flag to be a straight enabled/disabled option. It no longer provides a list of options for how auto dark mode is applied. This setting can now be temporarily enabled via the developer tools, under the 'rendering' tab. 

This version of auto dark mode seems to respect customisations made using `(prefers-color-scheme: dark)` and will enable the dark colour scheme before deciding whether to override any colours.

Like before, it selectively manipulates colours to achieve a minimum 4.5:1 contrast ratio for the given context, rather than changing colours uniformally across a page like a filter would. It generally seems to be quite competent at this, with the only contrast issues I could find being on pseudo-elements and background images. 

Interesting behaviour I noticed:

- The light border colour of the inverse Service navigation is changed to dark grey, but the background colour isn't changed, giving it less contrast than if no change had taken place.
- The background colour of inverse buttons was changed from white to dark grey, but the text colour wasn't changed.
- The icon of the Warning text component had its background removed but border retained. 
- Certain colours within inline SVGs are inverted (black to white, white to black).

Some issues that still remain:

- The coat of arms in the footer remains black (on dark grey).
- Pseudo-elements, like we use for various arrows and chevrons, remain dark grey (on black). 
- Checkboxes and Radio buttons are more visible than before, but still lacking contrast (at 2.59:1).
- Skip links and focused links become white text on a yellow background.
- Select dropdowns don't have visible arrows (appearing identical to text inputs). 

Generally this seems to be an improvement over what was here before, however. That it appears to still be actively developed and now surfaced more prominently in devtools may point to it being introduced as a user facing setting or feature in the future.

threadTitle: Handle thinking blocks and refusals in Claude responses
author: davidgisbey
text:
## Description

This is the first of three PRs moving the answer pipeline from Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5 to Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. It's groundwork. It doesn't depend on the private repo and changes nothing on the 4.5 models, so it can merge on its own.

Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 can send back two kinds of response the pipeline can't cope with at the moment:

- **A response that starts with a `thinking` block.** We'll run both models with thinking off. Even so, Sonnet 5.5 (on `between_tools`, its lowest setting) returns any note of more than a sentence or two that it writes before a tool call as a `thinking` block. Every step reads `content[0]`, so in the router that block would be read instead of the tool call.
- **A refusal.** Both models can decline a request with a normal 200 and `stop_reason: refusal`, which the 4.5 models never send. The router will also move to `tool_choice: auto` in the third PR, which doesn't guarantee a tool call. At the moment any of these would end up as a `NoMethodError` and an `error_non_specific` status, which hides what actually went wrong.

1. **Read Claude response content blocks by type**: finds the text or tool use block by type in all five steps (rephraser, router, composer, jailbreak guardrails and the guardrail checker), rather than taking the first block.
2. **Raise an error for unexpected Claude responses**: adds `ClaudeResponse.content_block`. It raises `UnexpectedResponseError` on a refusal, or when the expected block is missing. `PipelineRunner` handles that like an Anthropic API error: it notifies Sentry and gives `error_answer_service_error`. The guardrail checker turns it into the existing `MultipleGuardrail::ResponseError`, and jailbreak guardrails gives it the existing `error_jailbreak_guardrails` status.

## Testing

I ran the full suite in govuk-docker on each commit:

```
$ govuk-docker run govuk-chat-lite bundle exec rake
```

| Commit | Result |
|---|---|
| Read Claude response content blocks by type | 1,577 examples, 0 failures |
| Raise an error for unexpected Claude responses | 1,584 examples, 0 failures |

RuboCop and ERB lint gave no offences on either commit. Each component has a new test for a response that starts with a thinking block. I checked that all five fail against the old `content[0]` code.

Once it's deployed to integration:

1. Ask GOV.UK Chat a normal question, such as "How do I pay VAT?". It should answer as usual.
2. In the admin area, open that question. Its status should be `answered`, and the stored LLM responses should look the same as before.

## Risk

Low. The 4.5 models never return thinking blocks or refusals, so their path doesn't change. The only change you could see is that a malformed response now gets `error_answer_service_error` (or the guardrail error status) and a Sentry event, rather than `error_non_specific`.

## What I'd most like opinions on

Is treating a refusal as a service error right? It means a Sentry event and the "service error" message for the user. Some refusals will be triggered by users, so they could add noise to Sentry. A proper "refused" status would be better, but it's a new answer status that touches analytics. I'd rather see how often refusals happen in the evals first.

threadTitle: We have a route that exists only to mask out Local Links Manager-related electoral commision results
author: KludgeKML
text:
https://www.gov.uk/contact-electoral-registration-office is backed by the electoral commission API, contact-electoral-registration-office is also a valid local links slug, so URLS like https://www.gov.uk/contact-electoral-registration-office/richmond-upon-thames end up returning Local Links Manager info, which is less accurate that the Electoral Commission info. We therefore have a route which intercepts those calls and bounces them to the base search.

It would be better to retire the LLM backing service, or at least make it unreachable so that we don't need this masking route. It would also mean we could stop listing those links as bad in the Local Links Manager dashboard.

Introduced in PR: https://github.com/alphagov/frontend/pull/5333

We can pay it down when (eg) https://www.gov.uk/contact-electoral-registration-office/richmond-upon-thames doesn't resolve as a path.

Some history in archived ticket: https://gov-uk.atlassian.net/browse/PNP-9816

This pull request introduces enhanced support for dark theme customization across the application by allowing environment-specific configuration of primary and accent colors for dark mode. author: paulpod
text: ### 111 Online We looked at Dark Mode a little while ago, here is what we found. (There's a bit of conversation here, and compromise explored) Some users have mentioned it in feedback comments and user research for a long time. Some users were forcing dark mode on their browsers using a plugin. Using that plugin, it looks like this: Clearly if filled a need, but there are quite a few issues with it, so surely we could do something better. It's important to remember that users might not choose black (if given the option) for the dark mode background, as this can introduce harsh contrast issues. Their choice might be about the screen emitting less light overall, but not about maximising contrast. The first issue is the NHS blue on dark and/or black is a complete failure. We use the blue on text links, so that's going to be the first problem. Going all out for AAA contrast of the NHS blue is going to be a little bit nasty: Bearing in mind that the human eye is more sensitive to blue light than other parts of the spectrum, this seemed reasonable. I made a mockup with a visually comparable blue (along with using **darker images in dark mode**!) Following this I came up with a set of compromise colours that might work in harmony to recreate our page in dark mode while keeping the feel of it. This meant a new blue, that was perceptually close to the NHS Blue but passed at AA - **#348de0** This also introduced the need to detect the accessibility setting for high contrast, and offer a definite high contrast option: This can be detected in a media query using the css `prefers-contrast` eg. ``` @media (prefers-contrast: more) { .contrast-enabled-box { outline: 2px solid white; } } ``` I added a few more elements, with tweaked high-contrast versions and assembled a long page with a range of items. ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/49df334c-1e2d-40ef-8945-693a30e4cafa) Low contrast above High contrast above, note the addition of borders to the boxes to really pick those out, and the much brighter green, red (pink) and blue items. The big yellow banner was particularly problematic, so even though technically just bringing the colour across would "work" it is emitting far too much light for a dark mode.

author: LaurenMcAllister
text:
We're starting to look at an AI intent capture tool for NHS information and services - provisionally called "Ask the NHS". When designing the prototype we've been thinking about how best to introduce this new feature to users so they understand what it is, and have ways out of using it if they don't want to use AI. Having read around some of the emerging guidance in the public sector, we put together some overarching principles to inform the design. 

Broadly : There is deliberate friction in the design to ensure the user pays attention to what they are doing, rather than interact with the service in autopilot.

Specifically: 
* The user is made aware where AI is being used and what for
* The user understands that responses may be inaccurate
* The user understands the rationale/reasoning behind the AI response
* There is a feedback mechanism where users can report any inaccuracies
* The user needs simple controls to correct the AI if it's incorrect or goes off track
* There are clear routes away from using AI back to more traditional input
* There is a clear fallback option if the AI fails to produce a meaningful response
* Any error messaging takes account of the context and provides routes out to traditional input
* The interaction using AI is fully accessible
* The privacy statement clearly explains use of AI in the service, where any data is stored and the right to withdraw

The prototype is currently in UR. I'll report back any interesting insights/findings.

[GOV.UK's guidance on AI](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/using-artificial-intelligence-ai-in-services) says that we should tell users when we're using AI.

> ### Tell users when AI is being used
> Users do not always need to know what technology or software is used in a service to be able to access it.
> 
> However, if you use AI in your service, you must make it clear to users how this might affect:
> - their data
> - the outcome or information they receive from the service
>
> If you use an AI-powered chatbot, you must make sure users:
> - understand that the answers they receive do not come from a human and might not be accurate
> - know how to contact a human being
